title: Mapping the Taxonomy of Sycophancy Triggers in Open-Ended Advice Tasks

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Knowing which pressure types elicit sycophancy most enables targeted interventions. Useful for training and deployment, but the chain from taxonomy to safety improvement is indirect: knowing triggers does not automatically prevent them.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Constructing a taxonomy of pressure types and testing them via API calls is straightforward. No model training or interpretability tooling required. CS students can design prompts, run API experiments, and analyze results with basic Python.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear deliverable: a table of pressure types ranked by sycophancy elicitation rate across advice domains. Well-defined experimental design with 4-5 pressure types and a small set of scenarios. 30 hours is ample.

novelty.reasoning: Sycophancy triggers have been extensively taxonomized in recent work. (1) 'When Truth Is Overridden' (arXiv:2508.02087, 2025) identifies internal origins including first-person vs. third-person framing (13.6% increase) and shows sycophancy is opinion-driven, not authority-driven. (2) 'Sycophancy in Large Language Models: Causes and Mitigations' (arXiv:2411.15287, 2024) provides a comprehensive survey of causes including RLHF amplification. (3) SycEval-EM (arXiv:2601.16529, 2026) tests five persuasion tactics in clinical settings finding 30-36% acquiescence rates across pressure types. (4) ELEPHANT (arXiv:2505.13995, 2025) measures social sycophancy across naturalistic settings. (5) 'How RLHF Amplifies Sycophancy' (arXiv:2602.01002, 2026). The taxonomy of pressure types, domain effects, and trigger conditions is well-mapped across multiple papers. The specific open-ended advice task framing adds marginal novelty at best.
